title_en: Yuehai Company v. Cangma Company, Tefa Company, et al. — retrial of dispute over delivery of cargo without bills of lading, taking delivery, and agent's release of cargo in maritime cargo transportation

full_text_en:
Yuehai Company v. Cangma Company, Tefa Company et al. — dispute over delivery of goods without original bills of lading, taking delivery, and agency delivery in maritime cargo transportation (retrial)

Retrial Applicant (Original Appellee): China Merchants Cangma Transportation Co., Ltd.  
Domicile: 81 Kennedy Town, Sai Ning Street, Hong Kong.  
Legal Representative: Shi Jianxiang, General Manager.  
Agent ad litem: Zhu Xie and Shi Tongwen, Lawyers of Beijing Justice Law Firm.

Retrial Applicant (Original Appellee): China Shenzhen Ocean Shipping Agency (formerly Shekou Branch of China Ocean Shipping Agency).  
Domicile: Shenzhen Shekou Industrial Building.  
Legal Representative: Fan Jianxiong, General Manager.

Retrial Applicant (Original Appellee): Shenzhen Special Economic Zone Development Company.  
Domicile: Floor 03, Development Center, Jianshe Road, Shenzhen.  
Legal Representative: Li Jinquan, Manager.  
Agent ad litem: Zeng Yijun and He Zhengda, Lawyers of Guangdong Junxin Law Firm.

Respondent (Original Appellant): (Hong Kong) Yuehai Electronics Co., Ltd.  
Domicile: 4th Floor, Yuehai Building, 47-7 Connaught Road Central, Hong Kong.  
Legal Representative: Kong Hongbo, Director and Deputy General Manager.  
Agent ad litem: Li Ming, Lawyer of Guangdong Li Ming Law Firm.

Respondent (Original Appellee): Zhuhai City Haidao Development and Trade Company.  
Domicile: No. 29-1, Huazishi West Village, Nanhua Road, Xiangzhou, Zhuhai, Guangdong Province.  
Legal Representative: Jiang Youfen, General Manager.  
Agent ad litem: Sun Yanan, Deputy General Manager.

Respondent (Original Appellee): (Hong Kong) Huagang Development Company.  
Domicile: Room E, 9th Floor, Room 1, Waihua Centre, Shatin, New Territories, Hong Kong.  
Litigation Representative: Liang Jianhua.

The case of Yuehai Electronics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yuehai Company) v. China Merchants Cangma Transportation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Cangma Company) regarding a dispute over delivery of goods without bills of lading in maritime cargo transportation, and the case of Cangma Company v. China Shenzhen Ocean Shipping Agency (hereinafter referred to as Waida Company), Shenzhen Special Economic Zone Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Tefa Company), Zhuhai City Haidao Development and Trade Company (hereinafter referred to as Haidao Company), and Huagang Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Huagang Company) regarding a dispute over agency delivery and taking delivery of goods without original bills of lading, were consolidated for trial by the Guangzhou Maritime Court. After the first-instance judgment was rendered, Yuehai Company disagreed and appealed. The Guangdong High People's Court issued a final civil judgment on July 29, 1993. Dissatisfied with the final judgment, Cangma Company, Waida Company, and Tefa Company respectively filed petitions with the Supreme People's Court, requesting a retrial. The Supreme People's Court decided to hear the case on retrial.

The Supreme People's Court found after trial: On January 3, 1989, and February 21, 1989, Fuhui Company, a subsidiary of Yuehai Company, entered into two sale and purchase contracts with Huagang Company respectively, stipulating that Fuhui Company would sell to Huagang Company two batches totaling 10,000 sets of refrigerator components, with a delivery price of USD 250 per set at the seller's warehouse in Hong Kong, total value USD 2.5 million, and the buyer would be responsible for warehousing after arrival at the port of destination. After the contracts were signed, Fuhui Company, upon the entrustment of Huagang Company, on January 10, 1989, issued a written entrustment to Yuehai Company to handle the transportation procedures on behalf of Huagang Company for the 10,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets from Hong Kong to Chiwan Port, Shekou, Shenzhen. Upon accepting the entrustment, Yuehai Company delivered the first batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets and their accessories to Cangma Company for carriage in Hong Kong on January 26, 1989, and the second batch of 5,000 sets on February 21, 1989. Cangma Company issued four original bills of lading to Yuehai Company. The bills of lading indicated: the shipper was Yuehai Company on behalf of Huagang Company; the consignee was Yuehai Company. After the two batches of goods under the above bills of lading were transported to Chiwan Port, Shekou, Shenzhen, they were discharged by the Container Company. The goods record sheet of the Container Company showed: the entrusting party was China Merchants Barge Transport Company "Shekou" Co., Ltd. on behalf of Huagang Company. Because Huagang Company did not pay the full purchase price as agreed, Yuehai Company did not deliver the original bills of lading to Huagang Company.

On January 26, 1989, Huagang Company, through Ye Yongming, entrusted Tefa Company to declare the first batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets at customs. Ye Yongming, in the name of Tefa Company, issued a letter of indemnity to Waida Company, requesting to handle the delivery procedures. Waida Company gave Ye Yongming a copy bill of lading stamped with the import cargo delivery stamp. Tefa Company used this copy bill of lading to declare customs. The operating entity, consignee, and declarant on the customs declaration form were all Tefa Company. On May 3, Wanke Company, a subsidiary of Tefa Company, paid the customs duties for the 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets on behalf of Tefa Company, and customs released the goods. On October 23, Huagang Company and Wanke Company reached an agreement whereby Huagang Company paid RMB 500,000 to take delivery of 3,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets, and the remaining 2,000 sets were pledged to the Shekou Sub-branch of the People's Construction Bank of China, which paid the customs duties advanced by Wanke Company in the amount of USD 500,000 on behalf of Huagang Company.

On February 21, 1989, the second batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets carried by Cangma Company arrived at Chiwan Port. On the 22nd, Waida Company provided Chen Gang, an employee of the Container Company, with a copy bill of lading stamped with the import cargo delivery stamp for customs declaration. On September 30, Haidao Company, holding documents such as the import license and customs declaration form, declared the batch of refrigerator cabinets and accessories for import. Because customs duties were not paid, customs did not release the goods. Subsequently, due to the long-term storage of the goods in the warehouse, a warehousing dispute arose, and the goods were jointly auctioned by the court and customs.

On July 9, 1990, Yuehai Company filed a lawsuit against Cangma Company, claiming compensation for its loss of USD 2.15 million in purchase price and USD 550,000 in interest, on the grounds that Cangma Company delivered the goods to persons without original bills of lading. On December 31, Cangma Company also filed a lawsuit against Waida Company, Huagang Company, Tefa Company, and Haidao Company, on the grounds of taking delivery and delivering goods without original bills of lading. The Guangzhou Maritime Court held that the two cases were essentially a joint tort dispute based on the same facts and the same subject matter of litigation, and that the defendants in the latter case had an interest in the former case and were parties to the joint action, so it added them as defendants in the former case and consolidated the two cases for trial.

It was also found: The goods under the original bills of lading held by Yuehai Company were purchased by Yuehai Company from Goldstar Co., Ltd. of South Korea at a cost price of USD 190 per unit, with a total freight and miscellaneous expenses of USD 85,389 paid. Fuhui Company had already stated to the court of final instance on December 1, 1992: the property rights in the 10,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets sold by it to Huagang Company under the sale and purchase contract belonged to Yuehai Company. It fully supported the lawsuit filed by Yuehai Company against Cangma Company and would not separately file another lawsuit regarding the property rights in that batch of cabinets.

The above facts are confirmed by evidence including sales contracts, bills of lading, customs declaration forms, trial transcripts, and documentary evidence.

The refrigerator cabinets in dispute in this case were purchased and paid for by Yuehai Company, and Yuehai Company acquired ownership of the batch of refrigerator cabinets by purchase and succession. Fuhui Company, acting on the entrustment of Yuehai Company, entered into a contract with others to sell the goods; the relationship between them was merely one of trust and agency, and the ownership of the goods did not change. Fuhui Company also declared that the ownership of the goods belonged to Yuehai Company. Fuhui Company, accepting the entrustment of Huagang Company, sub-entrusted Yuehai Company to transport the goods to Chiwan Port, Shekou, Shenzhen, and the carrier issued a straight bill of lading with Yuehai Company as the consignee. This indicated both that the owner of the goods was Yuehai Company and that the final place of delivery confirmed by Fuhui Company and Huagang Company was Chiwan Port, Shenzhen. Although Huagang Company had entered into a contract with Fuhui Company to purchase the batch of refrigerator cabinets, Huagang Company did not pay the purchase price as agreed; after the goods arrived at the place of delivery, there was no lawful act of delivery. Yuehai Company has always held the original bills of lading. Therefore, Yuehai Company still has ownership of the goods in dispute and enjoys other rights and interests of the holder of the bills of lading.

Yuehai Company, as the owner of the goods and the holder of the original bills of lading, should be protected in its lawfully owned ownership and its right to take delivery of the goods with the original bills of lading. However, Yuehai Company failed to actively perform its obligations as the consignee, did not take delivery of the goods for a long time, and thus should bear the losses of lost profits and interest resulting therefrom. It should also bear corresponding liability for the loss of the second batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets.

Tefa Company, not being the holder of the bills of lading and having not lawfully acquired ownership of the goods, its act of declaring the first batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets to customs constituted a tort. Its act of disposing of the valid delivery documents to Huagang Company and Shekou Construction Bank for taking delivery had already caused the result of irreparable loss of the goods. Therefore, Tefa Company should bear full compensation liability to Yuehai Company for the loss of the first batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets.

Haidao Company, also not being the holder of the bills of lading and having not lawfully acquired ownership of the goods, its act of declaring the second batch of 5,000 sets of refrigerator cabinets to customs also constituted a tort. Although it did not take delivery of the goods due to non-payment of customs duties, its customs declaration act had created an obstacle for the holder of the bills of lading to take delivery with the original bills of lading, and was a cause of the auction of the goods. Its tortious act had caused harmful results, and Haidao Company should bear primary liability.

Cangma Company, as the carrier of the goods, received the goods shipped by Yuehai Company and issued original bills of lading. It should have safely transported the goods to the port of destination and delivered them to the holder of the original bills of lading. Waida Company, as the agent of Cangma Company, should have properly performed its agency duties. However, Waida Company delivered the goods to a person who was not the holder of the bills of lading. This act constituted a tort against Yuehai Company, and the legal consequences should be borne by Cangma Company and Waida Company jointly and severally. Therefore, Cangma Company and Waida Company should bear joint and several liability for the loss caused to Yuehai Company as a joint tort.

Huagang Company is not the tortfeasor identified in this case. The rights and obligations between it and Tefa Company and Haidao Company should be resolved separately by Tefa Company and Haidao Company in accordance with the law.

The court of second instance held that this case is a Hong Kong-related civil tort damages dispute, and the place of tort is within China. Pursuant to Chapter VIII of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the law of the place of tort, i.e., the law of the People's Republic of China, should apply. The court ruled: Tefa Company shall compensate Yuehai Company USD 992,700 and interest loss; Haidao Company shall compensate Yuehai Company USD 694,900 and interest. Cangma Company and Waida Company shall bear joint and several liability for the compensation to Yuehai Company by Tefa Company and Haidao Company respectively.

After the final judgment took effect, Cangma Company, Tefa Company, and Waida Company, disagreeing, filed petitions with the Supreme People's Court respectively.

Cangma Company's grounds for petition were: The buyer of the goods, Huagang Company, entrusted Tefa Company to declare customs and actually participated in the taking delivery and handling of the first batch of goods. In such circumstances, the judgment that Cangma Company and its agent should bear joint and several liability for Tefa Company's compensation to Yuehai Company lacks legal basis. The cargo owner Yuehai Company, in order to evade customs supervision, illegally bought and sold import licenses. Therefore, the loss it suffered should be calculated based on the customs valuation rather than the price at the time of loading the goods. The second batch of goods was not taken away by a person without an original bill of lading but was auctioned by customs and the court after a warehousing cost dispute due to long-term storage in the warehouse. Cangma Company and its agent Waida Company should not bear joint and several liability for the second batch of goods.

Tefa Company's grounds for petition were: The letter of indemnity issued by Ye Yongming did not bear Tefa Company's official seal, and customs declaration did not involve the ownership of the goods. Therefore, Tefa Company was not the person taking delivery of the goods. Yuehai Company held the original bills of lading but did not take delivery for a long time; instead, it assisted Huagang Company in taking delivery. This indicated that it had waived its ownership of the goods. Yuehai Company, knowing that the goods were taken away but failing to notify the carrier in a timely manner, should bear the loss for the expanded part resulting therefrom. Yuehai Company's claim had exceeded the one-year statute of limitations provided in the Hague Rules.

Waida Company's grounds for petition were: Yuehai Company was not the lawful holder of the bills of lading in this case. What Waida Company provided to the Container Company was not a delivery order, and Haidao Company did not use that delivery order either. The judgment that Cangma Company and Waida Company should bear joint and several liability for Tefa Company's tortious act lacks legal basis. The price of the goods should be based on the market price at the time of the occurrence of the tortious result. The judgment that Waida Company should bear joint and several liability with Cangma Company for the first batch of goods lacks legal basis.

Yuehai Company argued in reply: The bill of lading is a document of title. Yuehai Company did not agree to release the goods. The relationship between Yuehai Company and Huagang Company is irrelevant to this case. Yuehai Company could handle the customs declaration and delivery procedures through its domestic sister company. The first-instance court improperly mixed two different legal relationships: delivery without bills of lading and taking delivery without bills of lading. The one-year statute of limitations under the Hague Rules only covers damage and loss of goods, not delivery without bills of lading.

Haidao Company argued in reply: Its act of declaring the second batch of goods to customs was merely upon the entrustment of Huagang Company, and it had no tortious intent.

The Supreme People's Court held that: This case involves Yuehai Company suing Cangma Company for delivery of goods without bills of lading in maritime cargo transportation based on original bills of lading, and Cangma Company suing Tefa Company, Haidao Company, Huagang Company, and Waida Company for taking delivery and agency delivery of goods.

Yuehai Company is the named consignee under the bills of lading for maritime cargo transportation. A straight bill of lading is not transferable. Yuehai Company holds the full set of original bills of lading and has ownership of the goods under the bills of lading, being the only person lawfully entitled to take delivery. However, it is an offshore enterprise. Pursuant to Articles 18 and 21 of the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China, the goods under the bills of lading it holds cannot be imported without an import license and can only be re-exported or auctioned by customs. Therefore, its rights to the goods under the bills of lading should only be protected to the extent of re-export.

Cangma Company, as the carrier in the maritime cargo transportation, formed a contractual relationship of carriage with Yuehai Company as soon as it issued the straight bills of lading with Yuehai Company as the consignee. According to the terms on the reverse side of the bills of lading and by reference to Chapter IV of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, the carrier's performance of its transport obligations includes delivering the goods to the lawful holder of the bills of lading. For a straight bill of lading, the goods should be delivered to the named consignee. Cangma Company is liable for breach of contract for the losses caused to Yuehai Company due to the inability to take delivery with the original bills of lading.

Waida Company, as the carrier's agent, exceeded its authority by releasing the goods against a letter of indemnity and should bear compensation liability for Cangma Company's losses.

Tefa Company is not a party to the sale and purchase contract, but it declared customs and took delivery of the goods in its own name. Its conduct constitutes a ratification of Ye Yongming's handling of the delivery procedures. It should bear compensation liability for Cangma Company's losses.

Huagang Company, an offshore enterprise, violated the Customs Law by importing goods and actually took delivery of the first batch of 5,000 sets of goods. Its civil liability cannot be exempted, and it should bear joint compensation liability with Tefa Company and Waida Company.

Yuehai Company failed to timely take delivery of the second batch of 5,000 sets of goods that should have been re-exported, and it bears the responsibility itself.

According to the terms on the reverse side of the bills of lading, all disputes related to these bills of lading shall be resolved in a court of the People's Republic of China in accordance with Chinese law; regarding the carrier's liability, rights, obligations, exemptions, etc., the Hague Rules of 1924 shall apply. Yuehai Company did not make a claim to the carrier on the basis of the original bills of lading after the goods arrived at the port; instead, it filed a lawsuit only on July 9, 1990, which has exceeded the statute of limitations provided in the Hague Rules. Yuehai Company's contention that the Hague Rules do not apply to this case lacks sufficient basis. Therefore, its claim against Cangma Company should not be protected. As for Cangma Company's lawsuit against Tefa Company, Haidao Company, Huagang Company, and Waida Company regarding taking delivery and releasing goods without bills of lading, since Cangma Company's civil compensation liability to Yuehai Company has been extinguished, its claim should be dismissed. The original judgment contained errors in fact-finding, improper characterization, and erroneous application of law, and should be corrected. The retrial applicants' grounds for petition are justified and should be supported. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 184, Paragraph 1, and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Supreme People's Court renders the following judgment on August 27, 1996:

1. Set aside the civil judgments (1993) Yuefa Jingshang Zi No. 255 and 256 of the Guangdong High People's Court.
2. Set aside the civil judgments (1990) Guanghaifa Shang Zi No. 27 and (1991) Guanghaifa Shang Zi No. 06 of the Guangzhou Maritime Court.
3. Dismiss Yuehai Company's claim against Cangma Company.
4. Dismiss Cangma Company's claims against Tefa Company, Haidao Company, Huagang Company, and Waida Company.

The first-instance litigation costs for the former case shall be borne by Yuehai Company, and for the latter case by Cangma Company; the second-instance litigation costs shall be borne by Yuehai Company.
